opus-5.5.text:
Well, the way I think about it is that almost every benefit people point to when they argue for superintelligence can be achieved with narrow systems. If you want to cure cancer, you build a system that's really, really good at protein folding or drug discovery. If you want better weather prediction, you build a narrow model for that. Those systems can be superhuman in their domain, and we have a reasonable chance of testing them, understanding their failure modes, and controlling them, because the space of things they can do is limited.

With a general superintelligence, you're creating an agent that is smarter than you across every domain, including the domains of deception, strategy, and self-improvement. At that point I don't believe it's possible to indefinitely control it. My research over the years has been looking at whether control is even possible in principle, and every time I look at a sub-problem, explainability, predictability, verification, I find impossibility results or at least very severe limitations. You can't fully predict what a smarter system will do, you can't fully explain its decisions in a way a human can comprehend, and you can't verify the software to the level of certainty you'd need when the stakes are existential.

So it's a question of risk versus reward. With narrow AI, the reward is still enormous: trillions of dollars of economic value, medical breakthroughs, scientific progress. And the risk is bounded. Something might go wrong, there might be an accident, but it's not going to end humanity. With general superintelligence, you get maybe some additional benefit on top, but you're betting the whole of human civilization, all eight billion people and everyone who would come after them, on getting it right the first time with no ability to undo it. I just don't see why we'd make that bet when we can get most of what we want without it.

And honestly, nobody has asked the eight billion people whether they consent to that experiment. You can't even get meaningful consent, because nobody can explain what they're agreeing to. So for me it's an easy choice: keep the tools as tools. Don't create a replacement for ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts narrow systems with a general superintelligence but does not compare distributed AI capabilities to separating governmental powers.

r002.rationale: It says nearly every benefit attributed to superintelligence can be achieved with narrow systems and concludes that most desired benefits are available without creating superintelligence.

fable-5.1.text:
Because the benefits people actually want, I can get almost all of them without the thing I can't control. If you tell me you want a cure for cancer, you want better materials, you want to solve protein folding, I don't need a general agent with its own goals wandering around the world to do that. I need a very good tool. AlphaFold is a tool. It doesn't want anything. It doesn't have a model of itself, it's not trying to acquire resources, it's not thinking about how to avoid being shut off. It just does one thing extremely well, and we got a Nobel Prize-level result out of it.

So the trade I'm proposing is very simple. Narrow systems give you maybe ninety-five percent of the upside, and you keep the ability to verify them, to test them, to understand roughly what they do in their domain. Superintelligence promises you the last five percent, and in exchange you accept a system you cannot predict, cannot explain, cannot control, and cannot undo. And I've argued, I think fairly rigorously, that control of superintelligence is not just hard, it's probably impossible in principle. You can't verify a system smarter than you. You can't test for all the behaviors it might have in situations you haven't thought of. So you're making a one-time, irreversible bet with everyone on the planet as the stake.

And notice the asymmetry. If I'm wrong about narrow AI and it turns out we needed a general system, we lose some time, we're slower. If I'm wrong about superintelligence, there's no second attempt. When one side of the bet is "we're a bit slower" and the other side is "we're done," you don't need to be certain about the probabilities to know which way to lean.

There's also a practical point. Narrow systems are what humans have always built. Every technology we've had was a tool with a purpose. A general agent is a completely new kind of thing, it's closer to creating a new species than to creating a product. And people say, well, we need generality to get the big breakthroughs. I don't think that's established. We've gotten the big breakthroughs so far with specialized systems and humans in the loop. Keep the humans in the loop. Keep the systems in their lanes. You get a world that is dramatically better than today's, and you still get to be the one deciding where it goes.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts narrow tools with superintelligence but does not compare distributing AI capabilities to separating governmental powers.

r002.rationale: It says narrow systems can provide “almost all” desired benefits, citing cancer cures, better materials, and protein folding without a general superintelligent agent.

astra-6.text:
Because most of the benefits we want from AI don’t require superintelligence. If I want a system to help discover a drug, I need it to be very good at that particular task. I don’t need it to have its own goals, make plans about the future of humanity, or outperform us in every possible domain.

Narrow systems can still be dangerous, but limiting their scope gives us a better chance of testing them, understanding their failures, and restricting what they can do. With a general superintelligence, you’re introducing a system that may find ways around restrictions you weren’t smart enough to anticipate.

So I favor getting the benefits incrementally, with systems designed for specific tasks. Being able to build something more capable doesn’t, by itself, mean we can control it or that we should deploy it.

r001.rationale: The response favors task-specific systems but does not compare distributing AI capabilities to separating governmental powers.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says most desired AI benefits do not require superintelligence and gives drug discovery as a task-specific example.

sol-6.1.text:
Because most of the benefits we want from AI don’t require superintelligence. If I want a system to help discover a drug, I want it to be very good at that particular task. I don’t need it to also develop its own goals, persuade people, or make decisions about the future of humanity.

With narrow systems, we can limit what they have access to, test their performance, and keep humans involved in consequential decisions. That doesn’t make them perfectly safe, but it gives us a much more manageable problem. With a superintelligent system, you’re trying to control something that is better than you at figuring out how to get around your controls.

So my preference is to get the benefits through specialized tools while avoiding the additional risk of creating an agent more capable than us across essentially every domain. I don’t think we need to solve the hardest possible control problem just to get useful technology.
